 17-YO Builds AI Tool So Blind People Can Read Bank Statements & Textbooks More Independently
 Why should a blind person need someone else to read their own bank statement? That question led 17-year-old Yash Bhatnagar to build Visionably, an AI tool turning inaccessible PDFs into documents screen readers can actually understand. 
 By Nishtha Kawrani Edited By 
 Khushi Arora 
 16 Nov 2026 
 google-news Why should a blind person need someone else to read their own bank statement? That question led 17-year-old Yash Bhatnagar to build Visionably, an AI tool turning inaccessible PDFs into documents screen readers can actually understand.
 By Nishtha Kawrani 16 Nov 2026 19:18 IST google-news Follow Us
 New Update Yash Bhatnagar is using AI to make digital information more accessible to people with visual impairments. Photograph: (AI generated using reference)
 --> Imagine receiving your monthly bank statement, opening the PDF on your phone and trying to find out how much money is in your account. But no matter how many times you try, the information remains out of reach.
 Advertisment For a person with visual impairments, this can be an everyday experience. While a screen reader can read aloud the text on a phone or computer, it cannot always make sense of a PDF. The figures, tables and other information can remain inaccessible, leaving people dependent on someone else to read something as personal as their bank statement.
 Advertisment Add The Better India As A Trusted Source The same problem extends to school textbooks, government forms and even company reports.
 When 17-year-old Yash Bhatnagar learnt about this gap, he began wondering if technology could help fix it. A self-taught coder who had already built a couple of digital tools, he decided to take on a problem that many people had overlooked.
 Advertisment Visionably helps organisations convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that screen readers can navigate. 
Today, he is developing an AI-powered solution that helps convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that people with visual impairments can navigate using screen readers. But his idea goes beyond making a few documents readable. He wants organisations to rethink how they create and share information in the first place.
 From classroom tools to accessible PDFs
 Yash's interest in building things began early. Introduced to programming by his parents, he took a basic coding course on Khan Academy and continued learning independently, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.
 Advertisment His parents recall how he took to programming almost immediately. "Even as a very young kid, he was demonstrating a penchant for building new technology," they share.
 Yash developed Visionably after discovering how difficult it can be for visually impaired people to access everyday digital documents. 
Rather than treating coding as an experimental hobby, Yash wanted to create products that  solved problems for actual users. 
 Advertisment His first major project was LitGrades, an AI-powered flashcard generation platform launched in early 2023. After piloting it at his school, the platform grew to reach around 720 students, including learners from Ukraine.
 He then developed Silenttype, a real-time transcription tool that converted classroom lectures into notes that students could save in their digital libraries.
 In October 2025, while pitching the idea at IIM Ahmedabad, he began exploring how the tool could also help deaf users by transcribing spoken conversations and lectures.
 However, a conversation with the team there introduced him to a different challenge.
 "They told me that while they thought it was a good tool, there were more blind people who needed technology for OCR and converting PDFs into an accessible format," Yash recalls.
 The suggestion stayed with him. He was introduced to a few sample documents and began experimenting with ways to make them accessible.
 As he explored the problem, he realised that the challenge went beyond converting text into speech. Most PDFs are created without the underlying structure that screen readers need to interpret their contents.
 A document may look perfectly readable to a sighted person, with headings, paragraphs, tables and images arranged on a page. But without proper accessibility tags, a screen reader may not understand the reading order, distinguish between sections or describe visual elements.
 For someone relying on assistive technology, the result can be a document that is difficult, if not impossible, to navigate.
 Yash began working on a solution , initially with guidance from people in the accessibility community. One was Rashi, who works with V-Shesh, an organisation that supports people with disabilities and promotes accessibility.
 "The fact that persons with vision impairment have to struggle in educational institutions because a document was not accessible is something I have seen closely," Rashi says. She recalls students having to request assistance just to have documents read aloud to them.
 That experience made the problem particularly meaningful to her. As conversations between Yash and accessibility professionals continued, the initial prototype gradually evolved into Visionably.
 What makes a PDF readable to a screen reader? 
 Visionably works primarily with businesses and organisations rather than asking individual users to fix documents themselves.
 Yash's approach is simple: make information accessible at the source.
 "It would make sense to make a news article accessible for every reader, but the newspaper should make it accessible themselves," he explains.
 Organisations share their PDFs with Visionably, which processes them through its AI-powered remediation engine. In simple terms, the tool helps add the information that screen readers need to understand how a document is organised. The technology identifies and adds details such as accessibility tags, reading order and descriptions for images.
 These changes help documents meet internationally recognised accessibility standards, including the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 and PDF/UA, which outline requirements for accessible PDF documents.
 Once processed, the accessible files are sent back to the organisation. Yash says the turnaround can be around 48 hours, depending on the engagement.
 Building this technology, however, was not as straightforward as developing a tool that could extract text from a PDF.
 The AI-powered tool adds accessibility tags, reading order and image descriptions to PDF documents. 
Documents come in countless formats, with different layouts, tables, images and formatting styles. A system that works for a simple text document may struggle with a complex financial statement or a textbook containing several visual elements.
 "Because the number of PDFs on the internet is so large and the formats are so vast, it's very hard to account for every possible use case," Yash says.
 He worked through more than 1,000 test cases and iterations, regularly sharing documents with accessibility professionals and visually impaired users for feedback. He also received technical guidance from SaralX AI, a company working in the same space.
 According to Yash, the engine now succeeds on around 95% of the PDFs it is tested on.
 Crucially, the development process involves people who actually use screen readers. Yash says he has worked with a recurring visually impaired tester who reviews the documents and helps identify gaps that he might otherwise miss.
 Rashi recalls one instance when a visually impaired person tested an early prototype and pointed out several areas that needed improvement.
 "Yash said he wanted to meet again after a week. He sat through the night and by morning he had fixed everything," she says.
 For her, that willingness to act on feedback is what sets his work apart.
 Making websites easier to navigate for everyone 
 Document remediation is only one part of Visionably's work. The venture also conducts automated accessibility audits of websites.
 These audits help organisations identify issues such as images without alternative text, missing accessibility features and elements that do not meet WCAG requirements.
 The system uses open-source technology alongside AI-based adjustments to examine websites and generate reports highlighting areas that need attention.
 For instance, simply checking whether an image has alternative text is not enough. The description itself must communicate what the image contains. An image labelled only as 'image' may technically have text attached to it, but it does little to help someone using a screen reader understand its purpose.
 Visionably's AI layer helps assess whether such descriptions are meaningful.
 Yash's Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 identified 2,221 accessibility barriers across 30 major Indian bank websites. 
Yash also released Outloud, a free, open-source tool that allows people to test whether their PDFs meet accessibility requirements. Unlike some existing tools that are limited to particular operating systems or workflows, Outloud works across Windows, Mac and Linux.
 Users can run accessibility checks, examine the results and even incorporate the tool into their own development processes.
 The idea is to make accessibility testing more widely available, including to developers and organisations that may not have the resources for expensive assessments.
 From children's books to banking websites
 One of Visionably's first paying clients is V-Shesh, which works with organisations on disability inclusion and accessibility. Through this engagement, Visionably has begun remediating documents on a per-page basis.
 The venture is also working with Pratham Books to make 10 children's books on its StoryWeaver platform accessible, pro bono. Six books had been completed at the time of the interview, with the remaining four nearing completion.
 For Yash, making these books accessible is particularly important because their stories should be available to children with visual impairments too.
 Rather than creating separate versions that readers have to search for, the plan is to make the accessible versions available directly on StoryWeaver.
 Alongside this work, Yash has been examining how accessible some of India's major banking websites are. His banking accessibility audit is another attempt to bring attention to gaps that often go unnoticed.
 The Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 assessed 30 major Indian bank websites, identifying 2,221 accessibility barriers. Yash selected banks based on factors such as their popularity, size and publicly available website traffic data.
 The automated audit examined multiple accessibility criteria, including whether images had appropriate alternative text and whether website elements met established standards.
 Through a collaboration with Pratham Books, Visionably is making children's stories accessible to young readers with visual impairments. 
The findings were shared with the respective banks, along with reports outlining the issues that needed attention. Yash says Kotak Mahindra Bank and Punjab National Bank responded, indicating that the concerns had been forwarded to the relevant teams.
 He plans to reassess the websites in December 2026 and publish a comparative report to track whether improvements have been made.
 For Rashi, this kind of accountability is important because accessibility cannot remain an afterthought.
 "I have interacted with so many children who volunteer with organisations working with persons with disabilities, but Yash is someone who is doing it genuinely, because he truly believes in it and not because it looks good on an application," she says.
 His next goal: Make accessibility part of the design 
 Running a technology venture while studying in Class 12 is not without its demands. Yash spends around two hours on weekdays managing emails, reaching out to organisations, developing the product and planning new projects. Weekends are often reserved for longer work sessions and meetings.
 His parents, who are the company's directors because he is a minor, support him with business discussions and outreach. However, they say he makes the decisions for the startup, seeking their advice when needed.
 Yash hopes to make accessibility an integral part of how organisations design and share digital information, rather than an afterthought. 
Yash, meanwhile, sees plenty of room to expand. Over the next two years, he hopes to remediate at least 5,000 files and conduct 200 to 300 website accessibility audits. He is also exploring an assessment of shareholder and investor reports published by India's top 100 listed companies.
 His larger ambition, however, goes beyond fixing documents after they have been created.
 One conversation with a visually impaired professional who had previously worked in Microsoft Accessibility left a lasting impression on him. The person pointed out that accessibility is often treated as an afterthought rather than being built into the development process.
 That is a distinction Yash wants Visionably to address.
 "Our eventual goal is to become an accessibility design firm, where we don't look at accessibility as something that happens after files are created, but as part of the process when all of this actually begins," he says.
